usage: Koreans say 우리 (our), not 제 (my), for close family
noun + 예요 because 니 ends in a vowel
께 replaces 에게/한테 to honor an elder
께서 is the honorific of 가, raising the elder
examples: 할머니, 안녕히 주무세요.
Grandmother, sleep well (good night).
안녕히 주무세요 is the honorific bedtime greeting to an elder
우리 할머니는 시골에 사세요.
My grandmother lives in the countryside.
the honorific verb ending 사세요 (not 살아요) raises the grandmother
할머니께서 김치를 직접 담그셨어요.

께서 + the honorific past 담그셨어요 mark deep respect
nuance: 할머니 is your grandmother on either side, and in plain conversation Koreans use it for both the father's and the mother's mother; add 외- (외할머니) or 친- (친할머니) only when you must mark the side. It is built from 할- (an old prefix meaning a generation above) + 어머니 'mother', and it doubles as a warm, respectful way to address ANY elderly woman you feel close to, much like English 'grandma' for a kindly neighbor. The big trap for English speakers is grammar of respect, not vocabulary: a grandmother is a high-status elder, so the verb itself must be honorific — say 할머니는 사세요 / 주무세요 / 드세요, never the flat 살아요 / 자요 / 먹어요. Pair it with 우리 할머니 ('our grandmother'), not 제 할머니, because Korean treats family as shared. Compared with the polite stranger-address 아주머니/아주머님 (a middle-aged woman), 할머니 implies real old age, so misjudging the age can sting.

usage: use 우리, the inclusive 'our', for family
noun + 예요 because 지 ends in a vowel

께서 honors the elder as the subject
examples: 할아버지, 진지 드세요.
Grandfather, please eat (your meal).
진지 is the honorific word for 밥, and 드세요 honors the eating
할아버지는 신문을 읽으세요.
Grandfather reads the newspaper.
the honorific 읽으세요 (not 읽어요) raises the grandfather
할아버지께서 옛날 이야기를 해 주셨어요.

nuance: 할아버지 is your grandfather on either side, and casual speech uses it for both the father's and the mother's father; 외할아버지 (maternal) or 친할아버지 (paternal) pin down the side when it matters. It is 할- (a prefix for the generation above) + 아버지 'father', and like 할머니 it can respectfully address any elderly man you know. The spelling trips beginners because of the liaison: it is one solid word, 할아버지, written together — never 할 아버지 — and the ㄹ slides onto the next syllable so it sounds like 하라버지. The deeper pitfall for English speakers is honorifics: a grandfather outranks you, so the verb climbs to the honorific level (읽으세요, 주무세요, 진지 드세요), and 밥 politely becomes 진지. Say 우리 할아버지, mirroring 우리 할머니, rather than the textbook-literal 제 할아버지.

noun + 예요 because 니 ends in a vowel
께 honors the elder as the recipient

nuance: 외할머니 is specifically your mother's mother, and the prefix 외 (Sino-Korean 外, literally 'outside') is the key: traditional Korean kinship treated the mother's lineage as the 'outside' family, so 외- consistently marks the maternal side (외할아버지, 외삼촌, 외가). The contrast with plain 할머니 is one of precision, not a different person: 할머니 covers either grandmother loosely, while 외할머니 removes any doubt, and 친할머니 (친 親 'related by blood/paternal line') would name the father's mother. Because she is an elder, the same honorific rules apply — 사세요, 주무세요, 께서, and 댁 for her home — so do not flatten the verbs. The English-speaker pitfall is reading 외 as some negative 'outsider' label; it is just the historical word for the mother's side and carries no coldness at all. Note also 외할머니 is one word; do not insert a space.

usage: use 우리 for warm, close family
noun + 예요 because 모 ends in a vowel
subject marker 가 after a vowel
-님 makes it more polite when calling a female server
examples: 이모, 여기 물 좀 주세요.

usage: extended family beyond the immediate household
noun + 이에요 because 척 ends in the consonant ㄱ
subject marker 이 after a consonant
친척 modifies 집 directly, with no particle between

Its near rival is 가족, and the dividing line is closeness: 가족 is your immediate household (parents, siblings, spouse, children), while 친척 is the wider circle beyond it; saying 친척 for your own parents sounds oddly distant. The English-speaker pitfall is letting 'relatives' blur into 'family', and the grammar: 척 ends in ㄱ, so the copula is 친척이에요 with subject marker 이, never 가.

usage: warm, standard way parents refer to their son
noun + 이에요 because 들 ends in the consonant ㄹ
subject marker 이 after a consonant
count people with native number 한 + counter 명
examples: 저는 아들이 한 명 있어요.
I have one son.
있다 for possession; 한 명 'one (person)'
우리 아들은 축구를 정말 좋아해요.

우리 아들 + topic 은; the natural way to introduce your son

N이/가 되다 'become N'; subject 아들이
nuance: 아들 is your male child, the natural pair to 딸 'daughter'. usage: the warm, standard way parents say it
noun + 이에요 because 딸 ends in the consonant ㄹ
subject marker 이 after a consonant
native number 둘 with the noun; or 딸 두 명
examples: 저는 딸이 두 명 있어요.
I have two daughters.
있다 for possession; 두 명 'two (people)'
우리 딸은 피아노를 잘 쳐요.
My daughter plays the piano well.
피아노를 치다 'play the piano'; 우리 딸 + topic 은
딸이 그림 그리는 걸 정말 좋아해요.
My daughter really loves drawing.
그림(을) 그리다 'draw a picture'; -는 걸 nominalizes the activity
nuance: 딸 is your female child, the counterpart to 아들 'son', and parents habitually say 우리 딸 ('our daughter') with affection rather than the colder 제 딸. The standout feature is pronunciation: 딸 begins with the tense (doubled) consonant ㄸ, so it is said with a tight, hard onset and a high pitch — clearly different from 달 'moon' (plain ㄷ) and 탈 'mask' (aspirated ㅌ). English has no tense series, so learners tend to flatten 딸 into 달, which is the number-one pitfall here; practice 딸/달/탈 as a minimal set. Like all people, daughters are counted with native numbers + 명 (딸 한 명, 두 명). Grammatically, the final ㄹ is a consonant, so the copula is 딸이에요 and the subject marker is 이, not 가.

usage: noun + 예요 because 자 ends in a vowel
subject marker 가 after a vowel
the cover word when gender is unspecified
examples: 할머니는 손자가 셋이에요.

native number 셋 'three'; 손자가 marks what exists

옆에 앉다 'sit beside'; location with 에

nuance: 손자 (Sino-Korean 孫子, 孫 'descendant' + 子 'child/son') is your grandchild who is a boy — the son of your son or daughter — and its pair is 손녀 (孫女) for a granddaughter. The two combine as 손자 손녀 'grandchildren', and when the gender is unknown or mixed, Koreans use the softer collective 손주 (note: 손주, not the common misspelling 손자, for the gender-neutral sense). The key contrast for learners is generation: 손자 is your CHILD's son, whereas 조카 is your SIBLING's child — both can be young boys, so it is easy to confuse, but they sit one generation apart. The English-speaker pitfall is using 손자 as a unisex 'grandchild'; it is male-specific, so a granddaughter must be 손녀. Grammatically the vowel ending 자 gives 손자예요 and the subject marker 가.
